title: Spanner Bracket: Fewer Edges, Same Reach
pitch: Temporal cliques: every pair of nodes has an edge with one timestamp, and a path only counts if timestamps increase. The paper shows you can keep an almost-linear number of edges and still reach every pair within 3 hops (a 3-spanner). Single-file HTML toy: a tournament field (say 16 teams) where each pair plays once at a random round. The player drags to delete 'redundant' matchups. A live checker verifies that every team can still reach every other through at most 3 time-respecting hops. A button then runs a greedy temporal 3-spanner and shows how few games you actually need to keep the whole schedule connected. Framed as 'how few rumors/injury news hops does it take to spread through a league?'
discussion_why: Sports-schedule framing and a surprise ('you can delete almost all edges and nothing breaks') give moderate fit and a decent 'wait, really?'. Math and games tags are neutral in votes, so no bias applied.

title: Rumor Clock: Time-Respecting Line Movement Propagation
pitch: Model sportsbook line moves as a temporal graph: books are nodes, a move at book A at time t that gets copied at book B later is a time-stamped edge. Use the temporal-clique spanner idea (sparse edge set preserving short time-respecting paths) to find the small set of 'leader' book-to-book links that carry nearly all steam propagation within 3 hops. Output: a sparse leader graph from odds ingestion logs, plus an alert when a leader book moves so you can bet stale lines at followers before they catch up. Fits SharpLab's CLV tracking: validate by whether following the spanner edges beats naive stale-line hunting.
discussion_why: Directly about beating books to stale lines, which is core betting-server relatability, with a novel graph-theory angle that is a mild surprise. Betting and decision-theory tags are neutral in votes, so only a soft fit-based boost.

title: Shot Budget Poker: Spend Your Measurements Wisely
pitch: The paper allocates a limited quantum measurement 'shot' budget adaptively across anomaly-detection queries, spending more on borderline cases and fewer on obvious ones (reliability-aware allocation). Turn that into a single-file HTML game: you get 200 'looks' to classify 30 hidden hands/bets as sharp vs. square action. Each look gives a noisy coin-flip signal. Compare uniform spending to an adaptive sequential-test strategy (spend more on ambiguous ones, stop early on clear ones) with a live accuracy scoreboard. The player feels why adaptive sampling beats a flat budget.
discussion_why: A bankroll-style resource allocation puzzle fits poker and decision-theory, and is relatable ('how many hands before you read an opponent?'). The quantum framing adds light whimsy; no vote bias since all tags are at zero.

title: I Let an AI Read Server Logs Like a Poker Tell
pitch: Video concept built on autoregressive multimodal anomaly detection for microservices: an LLM predicts the next log line, metric and trace token, and flags what surprises it. Parallel it to spotting tells: a player who has acted a certain way for 500 hands suddenly bets differently, and the model's per-token surprise (negative log-likelihood) lights up. Walk through using next-token surprise as a universal anomaly score, then apply it to a sequence of NBA possessions or a poker hand history to catch 'out of pattern' moments such as a team suddenly pulling starters.
discussion_why: Poker-tell analogy and sports anomaly detection are relatable, and 'surprise equals signal' is a clean idea. Tags are neutral in votes so no adjustment.

title: Handling-Time Conveyor: Does the Line Jam?
pitch: Single-file HTML toy based on routing in line networks with handling times. Packets arrive along a line of nodes, and each hop costs a handling (service) time on top of travel. The player sets a routing policy (greedy forward, wait-and-batch, skip-ahead) and watches queues form. A live chart shows throughput against the stability threshold, so you can feel how handling time, not link capacity, sets the max sustainable arrival rate. Framed as a sportsbook: bets are packets, traders are nodes, and a slow desk at the end of the line causes the whole line to stall.
discussion_why: Relatable (lines at the window, bottlenecks) and surprising that handling time rather than capacity breaks the system. Whimsy from the sportsbook-as-queue framing. Votes are all zero, so no bias applied.

title: Elasticity of Alpha: Why Your Edge Dies When You Scale
pitch: Interactive toy based on 'The Elasticity of Quantitative Investment'. The paper models how returns respond to capital deployed and how strategy returns fall as capital grows. The player is a bettor or quant with a bankroll slider. Each unit staked moves the line or price (market impact), shrinking the edge elastically. The page plots the profit-versus-size curve and marks the elasticity-optimal stake. It sits next to Kelly, so you can see Kelly over-bet when your own bets move the market. Includes presets for a soft-book prop and a sharp-market side.
discussion_why: Directly about betting and bankroll sizing. Debatable: should you stake less than Kelly because you move the line? Surprising that more capital can mean less profit. Votes are neutral.

title: Why Hamiltonian Tours of Your Fantasy League Almost Always Exist
pitch: Video on asymptotic connectivity, hamiltonicity and toughness. In random or dense graphs, high toughness means almost surely a Hamiltonian cycle exists. Use a schedule graph (teams as vertices, games as edges) to ask whether a road trip can visit every city exactly once. Animate removing nodes (injuries, cancelled flights) to show toughness as how many pieces you get versus how many nodes you cut. End with a chess-knight-tour and tournament-scheduling payoff.
discussion_why: Sports-schedule hook and a surprising 'it almost always exists' result. Less betting-relevant, so moderate debate. Whimsy from tours. Votes neutral.

title: Partition Gap Oracle: Number-Theory Prop Lines
pitch: Build a Discord bot that treats the least s-gap of integer partitions as a random variable and lets users bet over/under on its moments, using the Baruah-Talukdar conjecture on moment asymptotics. The bot computes exact partition statistics with a DP, compares them to the conjectured closed forms, and shows where the conjecture holds or breaks. A game of 'beat the conjecture' with leaderboards.
discussion_why: Whimsical: betting on number theory is weird and delightful. Niche, so limited broad debate. Votes neutral.

title: Zero-Intelligence Order Book Casino
pitch: Single-file HTML limit order book. Poisson-arriving limit/market/cancel orders from a stochastic agent-based sim (the paper's agent-based half) drive a live depth chart. You place bets on whether the next mid-price tick goes up or down, and a toggle swaps in a 'neural' order-flow generator (a tiny hand-tuned conditional sampler standing in for the paper's learned component) so you can see whether you can tell real-ish flow from pure Poisson. Shows how order-book imbalance predicts the next move like a sportsbook line moving.
discussion_why: Relatable (betting on tick direction), surprising that simple stochastic agents reproduce market microstructure, and it mirrors how sportsbook lines move. Votes are all zero so no tag bias applied.

title: Focused Line-Shopping Estimator: FWALS for Props
pitch: The focused weighted-average least squares estimator picks model-averaging weights to minimise MSE for one target parameter (e.g. a single player's rebound rate) instead of the whole model. Build a props pipeline that averages across candidate regressions (pace, minutes, opponent, rest) with weights tuned per-prop, with a closed-form bias-variance tradeoff. Backtest against a single full model on historical lines and report CLV.
discussion_why: Debate over whether to average many models or trust one, a natural fit with betting and decision-theory. Moderately surprising that you should tune the model for the one number you care about. No vote bias available.

title: Your Brain Is Tilting Before You Know It
pitch: Video riffing on EEG-based motion-control detection and interaction entropy across high-order brain networks. Question: can a headset see you decide to fold or shove before you consciously click? Walk through how entropy of cross-region brain interaction rises just before a motion intent, then speculate on poker tells, esports reaction time and tilt detection, with a mock demo of a live 'tilt meter'.
discussion_why: Poker tells from brain signals is an instant debate starter: wait, really? It also raises ethics (would a headset be banned at the table?) and is fun and whimsical. No vote bias available.

title: Mosquito Bracket: Human-Vector SIS Outbreak Betting
pitch: Single-file HTML toy built on the human-vector SIS model (dI_h/dt = b·β_h·S_h·I_v/N − γ·I_h, dI_v/dt = b·β_v·S_v·I_h/N − μ·I_v). Sliders for mosquito biting rate, vector lifespan, and a spray/net control budget. The user places over/under bets on the endemic infection level before the sim runs. A live R0 = sqrt(product of the two transmission legs) readout shows the threshold at R0=1 where the disease either dies or locks in. It lets you feel how a small cut in mosquito lifespan collapses R0, because R0 scales with the square root of the loop gain.
discussion_why: Relatable (bet on an outbreak), surprising threshold behavior (sharp R0=1 cliff), and a prediction-market feel that fits decision-theory and betting. Whimsy from betting on mosquitoes. Votes are neutral, so no tag bias applied.

title: Why Disease Is a Two-Player Game: Mosquito Feedback Loops as Poker
pitch: Video framing the human-vector SIS model as a two-sided game. Humans and mosquitoes each infect the other, so the loop gain is the product of both legs and R0 is its square root. Control spend works like pot-odds: spend on the vector leg or the human leg, and the model shows which gives more R0 reduction per dollar. Compares to bankroll allocation and the Kelly-style intuition that you attack the weakest multiplier.
discussion_why: Cross-domain analogy to poker and resource allocation sparks debate about marginal-return thinking. Moderate surprise. Fits decision-theory and whimsy.

title: Elastic Rod Rolling Dice: Two Momenta Physics Toy
pitch: Interactive 2D/3D-ish Kirchhoff elastic rod, with the Hamiltonian picture on framed Lie groups (SE(3)) separating the body-frame momentum from the space-frame momentum. The user bends and twists a rod by dragging the ends, and two live arrows show the conserved space momentum versus the rotating body momentum. A bet mode lets players guess where a twisted rod will snap or buckle (a writhe-twist exchange) before it settles.
discussion_why: Whimsical physics toy with a prediction hook. Weaker fit to betting and sports, though the conserved-versus-rotating momentum idea is a pleasant 'wait, really?'. Neutral votes.

title: Early-Enrichment Screener for Longshot Picks (KANEL-style Ensemble)
pitch: Borrow KANEL's idea of an ensemble of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (learnable spline activations on edges) judged by early hit enrichment, meaning how many true positives land in the top 1% of a ranked list. Apply it to ranking thousands of prop or longshot bets so the top slice has the highest realized hit rate. Spline edges stay interpretable, so each pick shows which feature curve drove it. Evaluate with an enrichment-factor metric instead of AUC, since only the top-ranked bets get money.
discussion_why: Directly relevant to betting, because top-of-list precision is what matters, and the interpretable-model angle draws debate over black-box versus transparent models. Moderate surprise. Neutral votes.

title: Did Your Betting Agent Actually Read the Odds? Counterfactual Tool-Trace Auditor
pitch: Wrap an LLM betting agent (odds API, injury feed, bankroll calculator) in a harness based on the tool-trace auditing paper. Log every tool call, then run counterfactual dependence tests. Swap one tool output (move the line 2 points, flip an injury status) and re-run the agent. If the final pick doesn't change, that tool was decorative. Source localization points to which tool call the final answer really came from. The output is a per-pick 'receipt' showing which inputs the recommendation depended on, plus a flag when the agent cites a tool result it never used. Start with a Discord bot that audits the server's AI picks.
discussion_why: Betting relatability is high (are AI tipsters bluffing?), the surprise is that the cited reasoning may not matter, and it applies directly to decision-theory and AI trust. Votes are all zero, so no bias was applied.

title: Latent Regions of the Court: Spatial Regions + Temporal Signatures from Shot Time Series
pitch: Apply the scalable spatial-region and temporal-signature inference to sports data. Treat each court or pitch location as a time series (shot rate, xPts, defensive pressure through a game or season). Jointly infer which spots group into regions and what each region's temporal signature is (early-game, clutch-only, fatigue-driven). Compare the inferred regions to the standard zones (corner 3, mid-range) and check whether any inferred region's temporal signature predicts live prop moves. Also works on line-movement time series across sportsbooks, where the 'regions' are clusters of books that move together.
discussion_why: Sports fit is strong and the question 'are the textbook zones wrong?' is debatable. There is a small 'wait, really?' in finding clutch-only regions. Moderate whimsy. Votes are all zero, so no bias was applied.

title: Salt Table: Two Ways to Win a Crystal
pitch: Single-file HTML lattice or particle toy where a concentration slider sets the ion density. At low concentration, ions build a crystal one at a time (the classical route). At high concentration, they first clump into a disordered blob that later orders (the two-step route). Near the middle both routes run at once, which is the paper's 'pathways coexistence'. Add a race mode: bet on which route nucleates first, with a live odds readout computed from many fast Monte Carlo runs. Show a histogram of nucleation times split by pathway, so you can feel that the same bankroll-style parameter changes the way the win happens, not just how fast.
discussion_why: It's a gambling-on-physics toy with a visceral 'wait, it takes two different routes at once?' moment. It's whimsical and shareable, and the bet-on-the-pathway framing connects to games and gambling. Votes are all zero, so no bias was applied.

title: Can You Make an AI Forget a Bad Beat? (It Comes Back)
pitch: A video built on relearning-aware unlearning for knowledge graph embeddings. The story: you delete 'Team X's star is injured' from a model's knowledge graph, but fine-tuning on nearby facts brings it back. Use the tangent-kernel view to show why: the forgotten fact is still linked to neighbors in function space. Animate a small sports KG (players, teams, injuries) and show a naive delete, a relearn, and then the tangent-kernel-aware delete that stays gone. Close with the poker parallel of tilt, where you can't un-know a bad beat, and the practical question of whether sportsbooks' models can truly drop stale information.
discussion_why: The surprise is that forgotten facts return, and the tilt analogy adds whimsy. The betting fit is indirect, so it's a moderate rather than high discussion score. Votes are all zero, so no bias was applied.

title: Parallel Limits: Watch Your Bet-Sizing Multipliers Explode
pitch: A 2D bankroll-allocation toy: maximize expected log growth across two correlated bets under two exposure caps (e.g. per-game limit and per-book limit). Drag the cap lines toward parallel. LICQ (linear independence of active constraint gradients) fails as the angle goes to 0, and the paper's LICQ radius says how far you can perturb the constraint system before it breaks. The demo shows the radius shrinking live while the Lagrange multipliers (shadow price of each cap) blow up. The felt lesson is that stacking near-duplicate limits, like same-game parlays on correlated legs, makes your 'optimal' sizing numerically meaningless. One HTML file with canvas, draggable constraints, a live KKT solve, and a multiplier readout.
discussion_why: Relatable (correlated parlays and exposure caps), a mild 'wait, the optimum goes unstable?' surprise, and a clean decision-theory fit. Votes are all zero so no tag bias applied.

title: Self-Play Wobble: Noisy Gradient Play in Rock-Paper-Scissors
pitch: The paper proves lower bounds on stochastic first-order oracle calls for nonconvex-concave minimax even with variance reduction. Poker and RPS solvers are minimax problems, so the demo runs noisy gradient descent-ascent on a zero-sum game. Sliders set the noise level and batch size, and an optional SPIDER-style variance-reduced mode is available. You watch the strategy spiral around the Nash point, and a counter shows oracle calls spent versus the best possible rate. The point is that there is a floor on how fast stochastic self-play can converge, and extra cleverness only gets you so close to it. Single HTML canvas with a strategy simplex and a gap-versus-samples curve.
discussion_why: Directly touches how poker and game AIs are solved, and 'there is a provable speed limit on self-play' is a surprising claim that invites argument about GTO solvers. The orbiting trajectory is also visually fun.

title: Quarantine Lane for the Odds and News Scraper
pitch: Apply bounded provisional visibility to a betting-research RAG store. Newly scraped injury tweets, beat-writer posts, and line-move chatter go into a provisional tier that the model can retrieve only under a hard exposure budget, for example at most k provisional chunks per query and a cap on how much they can move a stake. They are promoted to trusted only after corroboration by a second independent source or after a time delay. This limits the damage from a poisoned or fake 'star is out' post that would otherwise flip a model's pick. It is built on top of the existing ingestion pipeline: add a trust-tier field, a retrieval budget, a promotion rule, and a log of what a provisional chunk influenced. A replay harness injects fake injury news and measures the fake-news-induced bad bets with and without the lane.
discussion_why: Fake injury news moving lines is a familiar sharp-bettor worry, and the AI-poisoning angle is topical. People will argue over how long to wait before trusting a scoop, which is itself a speed-versus-safety betting tradeoff.

title: How Many Shuffles? Slow Modes of Random Circuits
pitch: The paper analyzes the spectral gaps and slow modes of random Pauli rotations and random quantum circuits, i.e. which patterns relax slowest toward uniform scrambling. The demo uses a card-shuffle analogy: a row of n qubit-cards, with each step applying a random local rotation. It plots the weight distribution of a Pauli string (how many sites are non-identity) and overlays the slowest eigenmode decaying as lambda^t, with the gap setting the mixing time. A slider for n and for gate locality shows the gap closing, so you can see why some structure survives long after the system looks random. A side-by-side 'riffle shuffle until a deck is random' counter ties it to poker fairness. Single HTML file, simulated exactly with small Markov chains on Pauli weight.
discussion_why: The whimsy factor is high and the poker-shuffle framing is relatable. It carries a 'wait, it only looks random?' surprise, though the quantum math is a stretch for the audience.
